To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
, for a wide class of linear regression problems, SGD is at most a logarithmic factor worse than ridge regression, and, for some problem instances, SGD is much better than ridge regression.

(1) the generalization performance afforded by SGD is always at least as good as that of ridge regression (up to logarithmic factors), and (2) there are instances where SGD can generalize significantly better than ridge regression (up-to logarithmic factors).

(1) in a broad class of overparameterized least squares problems, the implicit regularization from SGD is always at least as good as the explicit regularization from ridge regression, and (2) for some problem instances, SGD can be much better than ridge regression.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that, up the to logarithmic factors, (1) SGD generalizes as well as the ridge algorithm, and, (2) SGD can generalize better than the ridge algorithm in certain cases.
the implicit regularization effects of SGD can be as strong as explicit regularizers in some settings.
the implicit regularization of SGD is as strong as the explicit ridge regularization, up to the log factor, for a broad class of problem instances.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the implicit regularization of SGD can be significantly more effective than the explicit regularization of a simple convex penalty (such as ridge) when the problem instance is sufficiently benign.
, for least squares problems, SGD can be viewed as an algorithm that automatically tunes the regularization parameter of ridge regression.
, in many cases, the implicit regularization of (unregularized, tuned) SGD can be much stronger than that of explicit regularization methods.
